translationRepairs: His father Ren Yue was a Hedong military adjutant and was repeatedly posthumously enfeoffed as Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent.
His father Ren Yue was a Hedong military adjutant and was repeatedly posthumously honored as Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent.
累贈太子太師 records repeated posthumous honors of an office, not a fief. 'Enfeoffed' is the wrong verb; 'honored' matches 贈.

When Tang Zhuangzong was Prince of Jin he widely recruited elite soldiers; Si at the time enlisted on account of his swift daring, took part repeatedly in campaigns, later became chief officer of the Changzhi Guard, and successively served as commander of the Fengsheng Army.

When Tang Zhuangzong was Prince of Jin he widely recruited elite soldiers; Si at the time enlisted on account of his swift daring, took part repeatedly in campaigns, later became chief officer of the Long-Duty Guard, and successively served as commander of the Fengsheng Army.
長直都校 names the Long-Duty Guard command, not a place Changzhi. The replacement matches the office and the chapter's idiomatic wording.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Director of the Secretariat.
He was posthumously granted the title Director of the Secretariat.
贈中書令 is a posthumous grant of the Secretariat directorship, not an enfeoffment.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Director of the Secretariat.
He was posthumously granted the title Director of the Secretariat.
The literal likewise renders 贈 as enfeoffment. 'Granted the title' is the correct action for this posthumous office.
An edict posthumously enfeoffed him as Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
An edict posthumously granted him the office of Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
詔贈太子少師 is an edict conferring a posthumous office, not a fief. 'Granted him the office' corrects 贈.
An edict posthumously enfeoffed him as Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
An edict posthumously granted him the office of Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
The same 詔贈 is mistranslated as enfeoffment in the literal. The office Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent is kept.
Early in Han he was made commander of the Fengguo Army, given the acting title Minister of Works, and concurrently prefect of Kang.
Early in Han he was made commander of the Fengguo Army, given the acting title of Situ, and concurrently prefect of Kang.
加檢校司徒 is acting Situ. Minister of Works would be 司空, a different office.
Early in Han he was made commander of the Fengguo Army, given the acting title Minister of Works, and concurrently made prefect of Kang Prefecture.
Early in Han he was made commander of the Fengguo Army, given the acting title of Situ, and concurrently made prefect of Kang Prefecture.
The literal makes the same 司徒/司空 error. 'Acting title of Situ' restores the office named in the Chinese.
An edict posthumously enfeoffed him as Director of the Secretariat.
An edict posthumously granted him the office of Director of the Secretariat.
制贈中書令 is a posthumous office by edict, not an enfeoffment.
An edict posthumously enfeoffed him as Director of the Secretariat.
An edict posthumously granted him the office of Director of the Secretariat.
The literal repeats the 贈/enfeoffment error for the same 中書令.
When Han held the empire he was given the acting title Minister of Works and made commissioner of the Inner Imperial City.
When Han held the empire he was given the acting title of Situ and made commissioner of the Inner Imperial City.
授檢校司徒 is acting Situ, not Minister of Works (司空).
When Han held the realm he was given the acting title Minister of Works and made commissioner of the Inner Imperial City.
When Han held the realm he was given the acting title of Situ and made commissioner of the Inner Imperial City.
The literal likewise misrenders 檢校司徒 as Minister of Works.
A gracious edict posthumously enfeoffed him as Director of the Secretariat.
A gracious edict posthumously granted him the office of Director of the Secretariat.
優詔贈中書令 is a gracious edict conferring a posthumous office, not a fief.
A gracious edict posthumously enfeoffed him as Director of the Secretariat.
A gracious edict posthumously granted him the office of Director of the Secretariat.
The literal has the same 贈/enfeoffment error for 中書令.
Wang Zhongyi came from Wancheng in Chen Prefecture.
Wang Zhongyi came from Wanqiu in Chen Prefecture.
陳州宛丘 is Wanqiu, the Chen prefectural seat. Wancheng is a different place-name.
Wang Zhongyi was a native of Wancheng in Chen Prefecture.
Wang Zhongyi was a native of Wanqiu in Chen Prefecture.
The literal likewise misreads 宛丘 as Wancheng. Wanqiu is the correct transcription.

In the winter of Tianfu year seven, An Congjin of Xiangyang rebelled and led troops against Nanyang; Jianchong then commanded more than a thousand foot and horse at Ye County; the Prince of Zheng, as Kaifeng intendant, sent Palace Commissioner Zhang Congen and Imperial City Commissioner Jiao Jixun with the capital armies to join Jianchong; at Huashan in Huyang they met Congjin's force, Jianchong gave battle and routed them, and for his merit was made regimental commissioner of Bo.

In the winter of Tianfu year seven, An Congjin of Xiangzhou rebelled and led troops against Nanyang; Jianchong then commanded more than a thousand foot and horse at Ye County; the Prince of Zheng, as Kaifeng intendant, sent Palace Commissioner Zhang Congen and Imperial City Commissioner Jiao Jixun with the capital armies to join Jianchong; at Huashan in Huyang they met Congjin's force, Jianchong gave battle and routed them, and for his merit was made regimental commissioner of Bo.
The Chinese names 襄州安從進. Xiangyang appears only later at 襄陽平, so the rebel's base here is Xiangzhou.
Early in Han he still commanded the palace guard, followed the campaign that pacified Yedu, and was transferred to prefect of Shen.
Early in Han he still commanded the palace guard, followed the campaign that pacified Yedu, and was transferred to prefect of Shen Prefecture (Shenzhou).
遷深州刺史 is Shenzhou (深州), not the 申州 already rendered Shen in s0108. The gloss prevents collapsing two prefectures.
When Pu and Yong were pacified and the army returned, the Hidden Emperor made Hanyin prefect of Jiang and acting Minister of Works.
When Pu and Yong were pacified and the army returned, the Hidden Emperor made Hanyin prefect of Jiang and acting Minister over the Masses (Situ).
檢校司徒 is acting Situ (Minister over the Masses), not Sikong, Minister of Works.
When Pu and Yong were pacified and the army returned, the Hidden Emperor made Hanyin prefect of Jiang and acting Minister of Works.
When Pu and Yong were pacified and the army returned, the Hidden Emperor made Hanyin prefect of Jiang and acting Minister over the Masses (Situ).
The literal makes the same 司徒/司空 substitution. The replacement restores Situ.
Xu Qian came from Yan Prefecture.
Xu Qian came from Yun Prefecture.
鄆州 is Yun Prefecture. Yan would be 兗州 or 燕; the original uses the wrong homophone.
Xu Qian was a native of Yan Prefecture.
Xu Qian was a native of Yun Prefecture.
The literal likewise renders 鄆州 as Yan. Yun Prefecture is the correct name.

In Han Qianyou year one he was Left Colonel of the Garrison Guard and, with Vice Director Ma Congbin, supervised ritual objects for Gaozu's tomb, saving materials and cutting costs by tens of thousands.

In Han Qianyou year one he was Left General of the Garrison Guard and, with Vice Director Ma Congbin, supervised ritual objects for Gaozu's tomb, saving materials and cutting costs by tens of thousands.
左屯衛將軍 is a general (將軍), not a colonel. The following 大將軍 in s0142 is a higher grade of the same word.

In the first year of Han Qianyou he was Left Colonel of the Garrison Guard and together with Vice Director of the Palace Storehouses Ma Congbin supervised the making of ritual objects for Gaozu's mausoleum, economizing materials and saving tens of thousands in cost.

In the first year of Han Qianyou he was Left General of the Garrison Guard and together with Vice Director of the Palace Storehouses Ma Congbin supervised the making of ritual objects for Gaozu's mausoleum, economizing materials and saving tens of thousands in cost.
The literal repeats colonel for 將軍. General is the accurate rank term.
Before long he fell ill, asked leave, returned to Wen, and died.
Before long he fell ill, asked leave, returned to Wenshang, and died.
歸汶上 is a return to Wenshang, not a place named Wen.
Before long he fell ill, asked leave, returned to Wen to die.
Before long he fell ill, asked leave, returned to Wenshang, and died.
汶上 is Wenshang, and 而卒 is sequential ('and died'), not purpose ('to die').
When his father's mourning ended he was recalled and appointed Grand General of the Right Thousand-Ox Guard.
When he entered mourning for his father he was recalled to service and appointed Grand General of the Right Thousand-Ox Guard.
丁父憂 is entering mourning; 起復 is recall while still in mourning, not after mourning ended.
When his father's mourning ended he was recalled to service and appointed Grand General of the Right Thousand-Ox Guard.
When he entered mourning for his father he was recalled to service and appointed Grand General of the Right Thousand-Ox Guard.
The literal likewise turns 起復 into the end of mourning. Recall during mourning is the sense of 起復.
One day he memorialized again, "Jing Jingsi has already been made prefect, yet I have not yet received Your Majesty's grace."
One day he memorialized again, "Tang Jingsi has already been made prefect, yet I have not yet received Your Majesty's grace."
唐景思 is Tang Jingsi. Jing Jingsi invents a surname from 唐 and is not in the Chinese.
One day he again memorialized, "Jing Jingsi has already been made prefect, yet I have not yet received the sage's grace."
One day he again memorialized, "Tang Jingsi has already been made prefect, yet I have not yet received the sage's grace."
The literal repeats the false surname Jing for 唐景思. Tang Jingsi is the name given.
Shizong assented; Hao and Liang had not yet fallen, and he was at once made acting prefect on the Hao campaign.
Shizong assented; Hao and Liang had not yet fallen, and he was at once made acting prefect of Hao Prefecture.
命為濠州行州刺史 names acting prefect of Hao Prefecture. 'On the Hao campaign' is not in the office title; 濠梁未下 only explains why the post is acting.
Shizong bowed his head and assented; Hao and Liang had not yet fallen, and he was at once made acting prefect on the Hao campaign.
Shizong bowed his head and assented; Hao and Liang had not yet fallen, and he was at once made acting prefect of Hao Prefecture.
The literal likewise recasts 濠州行州刺史 as a campaign title instead of the prefecture named.
At court Shizong, because he had been loyal to his master, pardoned him and appointed him Grand General of the Ruoxiao Guard.
At court Shizong, because he had been loyal to his master, pardoned him and appointed him Grand General of the Xiao Guard.
授若驍衛大將軍 appoints him Grand General of the Xiao Guard; 若 is the appointment particle, not part of a unit name Ruoxiao.
When he reached court Shizong, because he had been loyal to his master, pardoned his crime and appointed him Grand General of the Ruoxiao Guard.
When he reached court Shizong, because he had been loyal to his master, pardoned his crime and appointed him Grand General of the Xiao Guard.
The literal treats 若 as part of Ruoxiao. The office is 驍衛大將軍.
Zhang Ying came from Taiyuan; he was son-in-law to Commissioner of the Imperial Son-in-Law's Household Yongde
Zhang Ying came from Taiyuan; he was the father of Commissioner of the Imperial Son-in-Law's Household Yongde
The sentence completed by 之父也 makes Zhang Ying Yongde's father. 駙馬都尉 is Yongde's title, not Zhang Ying's relation as son-in-law.
Zhang Ying was a native of Taiyuan, son-in-law to Commissioner of the Imperial Son-in-Law's Household Yongde
Zhang Ying was a native of Taiyuan, father of Commissioner of the Imperial Son-in-Law's Household Yongde
The completed Chinese 駙馬都尉永德之父也 identifies Zhang Ying as Yongde's father, not as Yongde's son-in-law.

The Wu ruler knew him and repeatedly promoted him to acting Grand General of the Right Directorate of the Gate Guards; he served in turn as prefect of Huang and Yuan and wherever he went his rule was praised.

The Wu ruler knew him and repeatedly promoted him to the illegitimate office of General of the Right Directorate of the Gate Guards; he served in turn as prefect of Huang and Yuan and wherever he went his rule was praised.
偽右監門衛將軍 marks the Wu office as illegitimate in the Zhou historian's voice, not 檢校 'acting', and the rank is 將軍, not Grand General.

The Wu ruler knew him and repeatedly promoted him to acting Grand General of the Right Directorate of the Gate Guards; he successively served as prefect of Huang and Yuan and wherever he went his rule was praised.

The Wu ruler knew him and repeatedly promoted him to the illegitimate office of General of the Right Directorate of the Gate Guards; he successively served as prefect of Huang and Yuan and wherever he went his rule was praised.
The literal likewise reads 偽 as acting and inflates 將軍 to Grand General. 'Illegitimate office of General' restores both points.
